package_info.package_manager: Electron (custom build, not a public package manager)
package_info.package_versions: Unknown (affected Mac and Windows versions distributed prior to March 30th, 2023)
package_info.why_malicious: The 3CX Desktop App was compromised through a sophisticated software supply chain attack. Malicious code was inserted into the application's build process or its dependencies, resulting in the distribution of trojanized binaries to end users. The attackers embedded malware within trusted application resources, enabling information theft, secondary payload delivery, and targeted attacks, particularly against cryptocurrency-related organizations. The compromise leveraged the application's trusted status to bypass security controls and propagate widely before detection.

execution_context.trigger: At application runtime, specifically when the 3CX Desktop App is launched by the user and initiates resource loading routines.
execution_context.file_location: Within the 3CX Desktop App binary (Electron app bundle); malicious loader code in JavaScript files (e.g., 'app.asar'), which fetches and executes code from icon files hosted on a public GitHub repository ('IconStorages').
required_permissions: network (to fetch external resources from GitHub)
filesystem (to write/read temporary files or load resources)
process execution (to execute downloaded payloads or scripts)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Malicious loader code embedded in the Electron app (e.g., in 'app.asar') fetches a file from 'https://github.com/IconStorages/images/raw/main/icon.ico' or similar URLs. The file, masquerading as an icon, contains obfuscated or encrypted JavaScript or shellcode. The loader decodes and executes this code at runtime, enabling further malicious actions such as information theft or secondary payload delivery. (Exact code not provided in the report, but described as a loader that fetches and executes code from icon files hosted on GitHub.)
malicious_snippets.code_language: JavaScript (loader in Electron app); payload may be JavaScript or compiled binary code depending on platform
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the Electron app loads a resource file (icon) from a public GitHub repository. Instead of using it as a UI asset, the app decodes and executes embedded code within the file. This executed code can perform actions such as collecting system information, stealing credentials, or downloading additional payloads.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The application loads files with image extensions (e.g., .ico) from a public GitHub repository and executes their contents as code. This is highly abnormal, as resource files should never contain executable code. The use of a public repository for payload delivery is a known supply chain attack tactic, designed to evade detection and leverage trusted infrastructure.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Electron applications only use resource files (icons, images) for display purposes and never execute their contents. Executing code from files with image extensions is a clear violation of application integrity and expected behavior.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate apps may download and display icons or images from external sources, but they do not parse or execute code from these files. Any code execution from such resources is a strong indicator of malicious activity.
key_indicators: Resource files (e.g., .ico, .png) containing embedded executable code or scripts
Electron app code that fetches resources from public GitHub repositories at runtime
Decoding or evaluating the contents of non-code files as executable code
References to 'IconStorages' or similar suspicious repositories in resource loading routines
Obfuscated or encrypted payloads embedded within files masquerading as images

attack_chain.action: Malicious code is inserted into the 3CX Desktop App build process or a third-party dependency, resulting in trojanized application binaries.
attack_chain.leads_to: Distribution of compromised 3CX Desktop App installers to end users via official channels.

attack_chain.action: Upon launch, the compromised 3CX Desktop App executes loader code that fetches a resource file (icon) from a public GitHub repository (e.g., 'IconStorages').
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is loaded into the application's runtime environment from an external source.

attack_chain.action: The loader decodes and executes the embedded code from the fetched icon file, enabling information theft, credential harvesting, or further payload delivery targeting specific users or organizations.
attack_chain.leads_to: Exfiltration of sensitive data, compromise of targeted systems, or deployment of additional malware.

behavioral_signatures: Electron application loading and executing code from files with image or icon extensions (e.g., .ico, .png, .svg)
Runtime network requests from Electron apps to public GitHub repositories (e.g., github.com/IconStorages) for resource files
Decoding, evaluating, or executing the contents of non-code resource files within the application context
Unexpected process creation or command execution initiated by Electron app after loading external resources
file_indicators: Resource files (e.g., .ico, .png) with embedded executable code or obfuscated scripts
References to external GitHub repositories (such as 'IconStorages') in Electron app source code or resource loading logic
Unauthorized modifications to Electron app bundle files (e.g., 'app.asar', DLLs) not present in official releases
Presence of loader code that fetches and executes content from non-standard resource files
network_indicators: Outbound connections to github.com/IconStorages/images/raw/main/ or similar GitHub repository paths at application runtime
Unexpected HTTP(S) requests from Electron apps to public code hosting platforms (e.g., github.com, raw.githubusercontent.com)
Network traffic patterns consistent with downloading non-image content from image file URLs
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor Electron and other desktop applications for runtime loading of resources from external sources, especially public code repositories. Analyze resource files (icons, images) for embedded executable or obfuscated code. Flag applications that decode or execute content from non-code resources or make unexpected network requests to public repositories. Use file integrity monitoring to detect unauthorized changes in application binaries or resource files. Correlate network activity with resource loading routines to identify suspicious external fetches and subsequent code execution.
